name: I-tal diet

card.summary: The natural, mostly plant-based way of eating in Rastafari livity, followed by some for clean, additive-free food and a lean look.
card.note: Strict vegan versions in young children have been linked to nutritional rickets.

quick.overview:
I-tal (ital) is the Rastafari approach to food: eat what is 'natural', often organically grown, and avoid additives such as sugar and salt. Many Rastafari follow Leviticus-based rules that exclude pork and crustaceans, and some are vegetarian or vegan.[1]

People interested in appearance sometimes look to it as a whole-food, plant-heavy template in which food is unprocessed and skin and weight benefit from fresh produce. Research specific to the diet is mainly clinical nutrition reports rather than appearance studies.
quick.how: In practice the diet centres on fresh vegetables, fruit, provisions and grains, cooked without additives; strictness varies. The Twelve Tribes of Israel treat it as commendable but not essential, and the Fulfilled Rastafari leave it to the individual.[1]
quick.risks: A 1985 British Medical Journal screening of 42 Rastafarian children found that of 20 on a strict vegan I-tal diet, 7 had rickets; oral vitamin D treatment was successful in the affected children.[2] Strict vegan versions in growing children therefore need attention to nutrients such as vitamin D.

lead: I-tal (ital) is the dietary part of Rastafari livity: eating food produced and prepared 'naturally', often organically grown. Most Rastafari follow the Leviticus laws, avoiding pork and crustaceans, many avoid additives including sugar and salt, and some are vegetarian or vegan.[1]

Adherents also generally avoid alcohol, cigarettes and hard drugs. Practice varies between groups: the Twelve Tribes of Israel see the diet as commendable but not essential, the Fulfilled Rastafari leave it to the individual, and the Bobo Ashanti have stricter rules around food preparation.[1]

Outside the religion, people interested in clean, unprocessed eating borrow its emphasis on fresh plant foods with no additives, which can support skin and weight goals as any whole-food pattern might. The main published research is a 1985 paediatric screening that found rickets among children on strict vegan I-tal diets.[2]

chain: Whole, unprocessed plant foods without added sugar or salt
Leaner, clearer-looking appearance claimed by followers
angle.text: Followers describe I-tal as clean eating with fresh produce and no additives; any appearance benefit comes through the general effects of a whole-food diet.

infobox: Natural food; no pork or shellfish; often low or no salt and sugar[1]

paras: Rastas seek to eat food produced and prepared naturally, usually organic. Many avoid food from unknown sources or prepared by non-Rastas, and some men avoid food prepared by menstruating women, with some groups stricter than others.[1]

Not all Rastafari are vegetarian or vegan; some follow Leviticus only in part. The Twelve Tribes of Israel treat I-tal as commendable but not essential, the Fulfilled Rastafari leave it to the individual, and the Bobo Ashanti keep stricter rules, though they have become more welcoming of outsiders by the early 21st century.[1] Some Rastafari sell I-tal food commercially.[1]

A 1985 screening of 42 Rastafarian children under five at one inner-city London practice looked for nutritional rickets. Twenty children on a strict vegan I-tal diet were considered high risk and referred for biochemical and radiological investigation; 7 of the 20 had rickets (7 of 42 overall), and oral cholecalciferol treatment was successful.[2]

timeline.event: British Medical Journal reports rickets in Rastafarian children on strict vegan I-tal diets.[2]
